overview: The Minack is an open-air theatre carved into the granite cliffs above Porthcurno, about six kilometres from Land’s End, with the sea as its backdrop. Even if you never see a show here, it’s worth a look just for the setting.

The story behind it is lovely. Rowena Cade, who lived in the house above, lent her cliff garden to a local drama group to put on The Tempest in 1932, then spent the next fifty-odd years building and improving the theatre, much of it by hand over the winters with her gardener. It’s been a charity since 1976.

expect.title: Shows from spring to autumn
expect.text: There are performances between Easter and late October: plays, musicals and concerts, some put on by the Minack itself and others by touring companies. Watching a play as the light fades over the sea is a memorable evening.

expect.title: Daytime visits
expect.text: When there’s no show you can visit to look round the theatre itself. There are fewer visiting days in winter.

expect.title: Porthcurno below
expect.text: The beach at Porthcurno is right below, so it’s easy to combine the two.

goodToKnow.label: Weather
goodToKnow.text: Everything is outdoors and exposed, so bring layers and a waterproof whatever the forecast says.

goodToKnow.label: Before you go
goodToKnow.text: Check the Minack’s website for current visiting times, show dates and tickets.

week.slot: An hour to visit, an evening for a show
week.text: A daytime visit takes about an hour and slots easily into a beach day at Porthcurno. If you can, book an evening performance for one night of your week: it’s a very different way to spend an evening in Cornwall.

pairWith.why: the beach directly below the theatre
the cable station museum, a good wet-weather backup
the far western tip, along the coast

tips: For an evening show, think about taking a cushion and a blanket: the seats are stone and it can get chilly once the sun goes down.
Combine a daytime visit with a swim at Porthcurno, which is right below.
